You said:

as ai engineer i want to work on project in RAG and be a production project also deploy it using azure or aws so sugest a project for me that have good weight on my resume.

ChatGPT said:

Yes. For your goal—AI Engineer + LLM/RAG + real production deployment—I would not build another generic “chat with PDFs” project.

My strongest recommendation

Enterprise AI Knowledge & Operations Copilot

A production-grade RAG platform for company documents, policies, technical documentation, tickets, and operational knowledge.

Think of it as an internal AI assistant that employees can use to answer questions such as:

“What is the procedure for requesting production database access?”

“Why did service X fail last week, and what was the resolution?”

“According to the latest security policy, can developers access customer data?”

“Show me the runbook for deploying the payment service.”

The important part is that the system doesn't simply generate answers. It retrieves evidence, respects user permissions, cites sources, evaluates its own retrieval quality, and is deployed as a real cloud application.

Azure AI Search currently supports hybrid retrieval combining keyword and vector search, with semantic ranking on top; Microsoft explicitly recommends hybrid retrieval for high-quality RAG scenarios. Microsoft Learn+1

Why this project has strong resume value

A normal RAG project demonstrates:

PDF → chunks → embeddings → vector DB → LLM → answer

That is useful for learning, but it is now fairly common.

Your project should demonstrate:

Data ingestion + advanced retrieval + authorization + evaluation + monitoring + API + cloud + CI/CD + scalable deployment

That starts looking like something an actual AI Engineer would build.

On your CV, you could eventually write something like:

Enterprise AI Knowledge & Operations Copilot — Production RAG Platform
Designed and deployed a production-grade Retrieval-Augmented Generation platform using hybrid vector/keyword retrieval, reranking, document-level access control, automated evaluation, observability, and scalable cloud infrastructure. Implemented asynchronous document ingestion, citation-grounded generation, REST APIs, containerized services, CI/CD, and infrastructure-as-code on Azure.

That is much stronger than:

“Built a chatbot using LangChain and OpenAI.”

What I would build

1. Multiple knowledge sources

Don't limit yourself to PDFs.

The system could ingest:

  • PDF

  • DOCX

  • Markdown

  • HTML

  • CSV

  • technical documentation

  • company policies

  • support tickets

  • incident reports

  • FAQ

  • runbooks

You could create a realistic simulated company dataset if you don't have access to real company data.

For example:

/company-knowledge
    HR
    IT
    Security
    Engineering
    Finance
    Operations

/technical
    Architecture
    APIs
    Runbooks
    Deployment
    Troubleshooting

/incidents
    INC-001
    INC-002
    INC-003

2. Advanced RAG pipeline

This is where I would make your project technically interesting.

Query

Why did the payment service fail on August 12?

Pipeline

User
  ↓
Query understanding
  ↓
Query rewriting
  ↓
Hybrid retrieval
   ├── BM25 / keyword
   └── Vector search
  ↓
Metadata filtering
  ↓
Reranking
  ↓
Context compression
  ↓
LLM
  ↓
Answer + citations

Azure AI Search is particularly suitable here because hybrid search can execute keyword and vector retrieval together and merge the results using Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Microsoft Learn

This gives you something meaningful to discuss in an interview:

“Why didn't you use vector search alone?”

You can explain that lexical retrieval is valuable for exact terms such as:

INC-1842
API-502
AUTH-403
v2.7.1
DB-PRIMARY

while vector retrieval is useful for semantic similarity.

3. Document-level security

This is one of the features that can really separate your project from student RAG projects.

Imagine:

Alice → Engineering
Bob   → HR
Charlie → Finance

Alice should not retrieve:

HR_salary_policy.pdf

even if the document exists in the index.

Your metadata could look like:

JSON
{
  "document_id": "doc_182",
  "department": "engineering",
  "allowed_roles": [
    "engineer",
    "manager"
  ]
}

Then retrieval becomes:

query
+
user identity
+
permissions
↓
authorized retrieval

Amazon Bedrock's current managed Knowledge Bases also support document-level permission filtering through ACLs, which shows that authorization-aware retrieval is a genuine enterprise requirement rather than just a demo feature. AWS Documentation

4. Citations and grounded answers

Your assistant should answer like:

The payment service experienced increased database connection failures after deployment v2.7.1.

Then:

Sources
[1] Incident INC-1842
[2] Payment Service Runbook
[3] Deployment Report — v2.7.1

And preferably allow the user to open the exact source/chunk.

This is important because you're demonstrating grounded generation, not simply conversational generation.

5. RAG evaluation

This is one of the biggest things I would add.

Don't just say:

“The chatbot works.”

Build an evaluation dataset:

question
expected_answer
expected_source

For example:

JSON
{
  "question": "What caused incident INC-1842?",
  "expected_source": "INC-1842.pdf"
}

Then measure things such as:

Retrieval

Recall@K
Precision@K
MRR
NDCG

Generation

Faithfulness
Context relevance
Answer relevance
Citation accuracy

Then create an evaluation dashboard:

RAG Evaluation
──────────────────────────
Recall@5       91.4%
MRR            0.87
Context score  0.92
Faithfulness   0.95
Citation       97.1%

This is excellent interview material because you can say:

“I didn't assume my RAG pipeline was good. I created an evaluation set and measured retrieval and generation quality.”

Microsoft's current Azure AI guidance specifically emphasizes optimizing chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval and reranking when implementing advanced RAG. Microsoft Learn

6. Observability

This is another production feature.

For every request, track:

Request ID
User
Query
Query rewrite
Retrieved documents
Retrieval scores
Reranking scores
Prompt tokens
Output tokens
Latency
Model
Cost
Final answer

Then you can create:

                AI SYSTEM MONITORING

Requests/min       42
Avg latency       1.8s
P95 latency       3.4s
Avg tokens       2,140
Failed requests    1.2%
Retrieval hit rate 94%

Now you're demonstrating AI observability, not just ML experimentation.

7. Production API

Don't make the frontend talk directly to the LLM.

Build a real backend:

React / Next.js
       ↓
API Gateway
       ↓
FastAPI
       ↓
RAG Orchestrator
 ┌─────┼─────────────┐
 ↓     ↓             ↓
Search  LLM       Database

Endpoints could include:

http
POST /api/chat
POST /api/documents
GET  /api/documents
GET  /api/conversations
GET  /api/health
GET  /api/evaluation

8. Asynchronous ingestion

This is another production-style component.

Don't make the user wait while a 200-page PDF is processed.

Instead:

Upload
   ↓
Object Storage
   ↓
Queue
   ↓
Ingestion Worker
   ↓
Parser
   ↓
Chunking
   ↓
Embedding
   ↓
Index

So the frontend can show:

Document uploaded

Processing...
██████████████░░ 78%

Status: Indexing

This makes your architecture much closer to an actual production system.

Azure's own current RAG documentation describes the combination of Azure AI Search and Azure OpenAI for RAG, and Microsoft's sample architectures use containerized APIs and separate ingestion/application components. Microsoft Learn

10. Infrastructure as Code

This is a big resume booster.

Don't manually create everything in Azure.

Use:

Terraform

or Bicep.

Your repository could contain:

infra/
    main.tf
    variables.tf
    outputs.tf
    search.tf
    storage.tf
    container_app.tf
    monitoring.tf

Then:

Bash
terraform apply

and your infrastructure gets created.

That shows you understand cloud engineering, not just AI.

Your GitHub repository:

After the RAG system works, add an agent.

For example:

User:
Why did payment service fail?

Agent

This moves your project toward:

RAG → Agentic RAG → production AI system

Azure's current AI Search guidance distinguishes classic RAG from newer agentic retrieval approaches and notes that agentic retrieval can decompose complex queries and improve retrieval for conversational workloads. Microsoft Learn+1

Don't make the project huge from day one.

Build it in four stages.

Stage 1 — Core RAG

Azure vs AWS for this project

Both are good.

Azure

I would use:

Azure OpenAI
Azure AI Search
Azure Blob Storage
Azure Container Apps
Azure Key Vault
Azure Monitor

This gives you a very coherent stack specifically for enterprise RAG. Azure AI Search's current capabilities include hybrid search and semantic ranking, which are particularly useful for demonstrating advanced retrieval. Microsoft Learn+1

AWS

A comparable version would use:

Amazon Bedrock
Bedrock Knowledge Bases
S3
ECS/Fargate
OpenSearch
RDS
CloudWatch
IAM

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases currently supports managed ingestion/retrieval, hybrid search, reranking, citations, multimodal retrieval capabilities, and ACL-based document filtering. AWS Documentation+2AWS Documentation+2

For your first serious RAG project, I would choose Azure.

Then, once the Azure version is complete, you could create a second deployment architecture on AWS. That would be particularly valuable for an AI Engineer CV because you'd be able to demonstrate cloud portability rather than being locked into one provider.

That is the kind of project where an interviewer can ask you:

“Why hybrid search?”

“Why did you choose this chunking strategy?”

“How did you evaluate retrieval?”

“How do you prevent unauthorized documents from entering the context?”

“How do you detect hallucinations?”

“How do you reduce latency?”

“How do you monitor token cost?”

“How would you scale ingestion?”

“Why Azure AI Search instead of a standalone vector database?”

And you can answer with your own implementation and measurements, rather than theoretical knowledge.

Resume impact

I would rank the project roughly like this:

ProjectResume value
Chatbot with PDF★★☆☆☆
Basic RAG app★★★☆☆
RAG + hybrid search + reranking★★★★☆

The key is not the number of technologies. The key is being able to prove that your system works.

For example, having a GitHub README showing:

Recall@5:        93.2%
MRR:             0.89
Faithfulness:    95.4%
P95 latency:     2.8s
Cost/query:      $0.012

is much more impressive than a README saying:

“I used LangChain, FAISS and GPT.”

Project name

I'd give it a professional name rather than calling it simply “RAG chatbot.”

NexusAI — Enterprise Knowledge & Operations Copilot

That gives you a project you can present as an actual AI platform, not a tutorial application.
